Chvátal's Art Gallery Theorem

CountingGraph TheoryAlgorithms
Game: Pick as few corners as possible so that every spot inside the polygon can be seen from one of them.
How to play: Click one corner and then another to draw a diagonal that stays inside and never crosses another. Keep going until no more fit, then look at the marked corners.

Mode
Look for the math

A guard standing at a corner of a strange, bent gallery cannot always see every corner of the room. The surprise is that no matter how crooked the polygon is, you never need more than about a third of its corners — and some galleries really need that many. This page shows the idea behind Chvatal's art gallery theorem.

Cut it into triangles first

Any simple polygon can be cut up by diagonals that lie inside it and never cross. A polygon with n corners needs exactly n − 3 diagonals, and the result has n − 2 triangles. This is the first step of the proof, and it is what you are doing when you draw diagonals: the applet knows it is finished once the count reaches n − 3. The logic test checked this for every triangulation of every polygon of 4 to 9 corners, and for a fan triangulation all the way up to the applet's limit of 40.

Colour with three colours

Now colour every corner using three colours so that each little triangle has all three. Start with any triangle and colour its corners; every triangle next door shares two of them, so its third corner is forced to take the only colour left. The triangles join up like the nodes of a tree — there is no loop that could bring back a conflicting colour — so the colouring always works. Every triangle has a corner of each colour, so standing at every corner of one colour sees every triangle. That is the key insight of Steve Fisk's proof, which the applet carries out for you.

Choose the smallest pile

Suppose the three colours are used B, R and G times. They colour all the corners, so B + R + G = n. One of them must be the smallest, and three times that smallest number cannot exceed n: 3B ≤ n. By the pigeonhole principle the smallest class has at most floor(n/3) corners. Those are the marked corners on the board. The logic test verified on all 624 triangulations of 4- to 9-gons that every triangle contains a marked corner and that the marked set never exceeds floor(n/3).

Could you do better?

The bound is tight, so the answer really is floor(n/3) in the worst case. A comb-shaped polygon with n triangular teeth has so many tucked-away pockets that each guard can watch only a few of them; you need at least floor(n/3) corners, and the three-colouring method finds exactly that many. Convex polygons are much easier — one corner sees the whole room — but the question asks about the worst polygon of all. This is why the applet lets you both rearrange the corners and draw the diagonals: you can try to build a stubborn gallery yourself.

Try a corner count that is a multiple of three, make a comb with that many teeth, and see whether the marked corners are exactly one third of them.
